ImageDescription.value:
An elegant German fastback coupé of the Audi 100 Coupé S series (C1 generation) in a period-correct light blue metallic finish, photographed in the extensive grounds of the historic Château La Borde en Sologne in Vernou-en-Sologne, France.

Unveiled as a prototype in the autumn of 1969 at the International Motor Show (IAA) and produced from 1970 onwards, the Coupé S is considered one of the most brilliant design milestones in the history of the Ingolstadt-based brand, introducing Audi to the world of upscale automotive lifestyle for the very first time. The fascinating lines of the four-seater, initiated by Ludwig Kraus, with its gently sloping rear section and distinctive ventilation louvres in the C-pillar, strongly resemble classic Italian sports car designs of the era, most notably the Fiat Dino or the Maserati Ghibli Coupé.

With its twin-headlight front end and the charismatic crease line in its sheet metal body, the car became an exclusive status symbol for a design-oriented, wealthy clientele seeking a stylish alternative to the traditional, conservative luxury-class saloons. Between 1970 and 1976, exactly 30,687 units left the factory. The model shown here masterfully combines the progressive, optimistic spirit of the early 1970s with traditional engineering prowess and, due to its rarity, is considered a top-tier collector's item today.

I. Technical Development and Design Features

  • Construction & Design Influences: The Audi 100 Coupé S is based on the floorpan of the Audi 100 saloon (C1), shortened by 11.5 centimetres. The visual proximity to Italian Grand Tourer design was the result of a bold decision by Chief Development Engineer Ludwig Kraus. The sweeping fastback tail with its characteristic five ventilation slots in the C-pillar brought a touch of Turin to Ingolstadt. In the contemporary press, the car was frequently described as a "pike in a carp pond" within the rather conservative German automotive landscape.
  • Engine & Technology: The coupé is powered by a variant of the saloon's four-cylinder in-line engine, bored out to 1,871 cc. In the initial version (until 1971), twin Solex register carburettors delivered a sporty 115 PS (85 kW), granting the lightweight vehicle, weighing just under 1,100 kg, an impressive top speed of 185 km/h for the time. From autumn 1971, power output was adjusted to a single register carburettor producing 112 PS (82 kW) in order to meet emission and fuel consumption standards.
  • Chassis & Braking System: A technical peculiarity of the early C1 models was the inboard disc brakes at the front axle. These were mounted directly to the gearbox to reduce unsprung mass at the wheels (they were relocated to the conventional position at the wheel hubs only for the 1975 model year, in the late summer of 1974). The combination of front-wheel drive, a robust rigid axle with trailing arms and a transverse torsion bar at the rear, along with precise steering, provided the coupé with unexpectedly agile and secure handling characteristics.

II. Social, Economic and Cultural History

  • The Secretly Developed Saviour of the Brand (The Wolfsburg Blockade): Economically, the existence of this vehicle is nothing short of a miracle. Following Volkswagen's complete takeover of Auto Union in 1966, VW Chief Executive Heinrich Nordhoff imposed a strict production ban on independent new models in Ingolstadt. According to the wishes of the corporate leadership, Audi was meant to die out and serve merely as an anonymous overflow plant for assembling the booming VW Beetle. However, Chief Development Engineer Ludwig Kraus secretly defied these orders: working late into the evenings and nights, he covertly designed the Audi 100 saloon. When he presented the finished car to the stunned VW board, they were so convinced by its market potential that they reluctantly approved series production. The Audi 100 became a massive success, saved the independence and survival of the Audi brand, and laid the financial foundation for developing the highly emotive Coupé S.
  • From Everyday Classic to Absolute Rarity: While the saloons rolled off the assembly lines in large numbers, manufacturing the coupé at the Neckarsulm plant was significantly more complex. With exactly 30,687 units built, the car remained an exclusive sight on the roads. Due to the lack of adequate rust protection at the time and the use of inferior recycled sheet metal, the surviving population shrank dramatically. Out of the original production run, it is estimated that only a low three-figure number of roadworthy, original-condition examples exist worldwide today.
  • The "Poor Man's Porsche": The car struck a chord with the aspiring middle class of the early 1970s. It offered the visual allure of an expensive sports car, yet remained affordable to maintain thanks to the mass-production technology shared with the saloon, while providing genuine space for four people and their luggage – a perfect automobile for stylish weekend getaways.

III. Pop Culture, Celebrity and Everyday Myth

  • The Automobile of the Professionals: In the society of the era, the Audi 100 was regarded as the typical status symbol of the upper-middle class, particularly favoured by self-employed professionals such as architects, doctors, tax consultants, and lawyers. Those who wanted to project success, but wished to avoid the ostentatious charm of Mercedes-Benz or the sportiness of BMW (which was perceived as aggressive at the time), chose Audi. The brand stood for a progressive spirit, technical intelligence, and a cultivated, unobtrusive affluence. While the saloon was the respectable workhorse for the middle class on long motorway journeys, the Coupé S crowned the range: it added a heavy dose of Italian dolce vita to the rational "Vorsprung durch Technik", proving that its owner possessed taste without losing touch with reality. At its market launch in 1970, the base price of the noble fastback stood at exactly 14,400 Deutsche Marks. By comparison, this was nearly twice as expensive as a standard VW Beetle of the time and noticeably dearer than a Ford Capri. Those who treated themselves to the newly introduced three-speed automatic transmission and additional extras in October 1971 easily broke the 15,000 Mark barrier.
  • Celebrity and the British Rock Idol: Although the car was primarily a success in Germany and continental Europe, a very special example found its way to England to a genuine music legend. Jethro Tull frontman Ian Anderson purchased a brand-new Audi 100 Coupé S in the early 1970s. The eccentric flautist and rock star appreciated the avant-garde design and used the car extensively for his travels away from the concert stages, giving the model an unexpected touch of progressive rock glamour in the UK.
  • The Visual Kinship to British Luxury: A wonderful piece of automotive design history connects the Coupé S with the absolute luxury class. When the vehicle entered the market, car enthusiasts worldwide rubbed their eyes: the strikingly sloping rear section with its characteristic ventilation louvres in the C-pillar bore a stunning resemblance to the legendary British sports car, the 1967 Aston Martin DBS. This similarity was so conspicuous that the Audi 100 Coupé S quickly earned the charming colloquial nickname "the poor man's Aston Martin" in both popular parlance and the motoring press. It proved that the Ingolstadt design team led by Ludwig Kraus had created a highly emotional masterpiece capable of visually holding its own against the most exclusive league of the sports car world.
  • Unexpected Success in Endurance Rallies: Although the Coupé S, like the entire C1 line, was never conceived as a purebred racing car, it was deployed in private and production-based motorsport due to its excellent front-wheel-drive chassis and balanced weight distribution. In demanding European rallies of the early 1970s (such as the Rally Niedersachsen or national reliability trials), privateer drivers secured numerous class victories with the Coupé S against established rear-wheel-drive competition. Its reliability on ice and mud cemented the reputation of Ingolstadt engineering.
  • Connection to the Modern Audi A7: The design heritage of this vehicle reaches right into the present day. When Audi introduced the modern Audi A7 Sportback in 2010, the designers explicitly emphasised that the distinctively sloping roofline and the side window graphics were directly inspired by the classic Audi 100 Coupé S of the 1970s.
